content: Discussion thread for #announce > Lean Kernel Arena
Is it necessary to use nix develop to run the tests locally?

No, you can install the python dependencies any other way.

Or, if your goal is to test your own checkers, you can download the tarball that's linked from the front page. It contains the built tests.
I figured out what the issue was. I needed to set perf_event_paranoid lower.

It looks like the one false positive being reported for Nanoda is that it accepts non-propositional theorem declarations. Is this really that important from a soundness perspective? My understanding is that at the level of type checking, the difference between a definition and a theorem is essentially cosmetic.

It's borderline of course - you cannot prove false with it. On the other hand it is an invariant checked by the official kernel (and also lean4lean). So in the interest of compatibility, and with not much more to rely on for a specification than the official kernel, it'd say it's probably best if checkers agree on these cosmetic things.

If Chris Bailey has reasons to not implement this check I can also add a test label and opt his checker out, so that it doesn't look red. These things are still settling, hence the “under construction” label. The other red tests are also just temporary things.

I expect we'll encounter more corner cases where it's unclear if some behavior of the official kernel is just an implementation choice, or part of the checker contract, and hopefully we'll learn something useful from them.

I just want to say that I think this is a great effort! I've been interested in writing a checker for a while now and think this will be a helpful and motivating resource. I've also been working a bit on a somewhat "beginner friendly" blog post about the kernel, ZFC equiconsistency, etc. and this is great to point to as a unified location for these external checkers.

I have implemented the non-propositional theorem check. Some other odds and ends I have locally for the json move are an unsafe_permit_all_axioms config option which was discussed elsewhere as a "nice to have" for this kind of application, a more harsh restriction on duplicate names, which James Hanson brought up in another thread, and a config option pp_axioms that defaults to true, and pretty-prints the used axioms at the end of type checking.
What is the input to these kernels? Lean code (pre-compiled)? oleans? Exported proofs? I ask, because we know some input forms are more susceptible to hacks.

Also, as Comparator becomes more mature (and more needed as vibe coded proofs become common), it would be useful to make a version of this site which also focuses on the Comparator interface (with a challenge file). Then one could add SafeVerify to the list, Comparator with different external checkers (when that is available), and lean4checker (to highlight that there are a lot of things that lean4checker doesn't check like axioms, environment hacks, and changes to the code like removing the theorem you want to prove). Then you can also add other sorts of Lean hacks and bugs to the tests, such as all those used in the Comparator/safe verify tests, the ones @James E Hanson recently uncovered (which don't effect Comparator, but do effect SafeVerify), and maybe even attempted hacks which attempt to change files on the file system.

Jason Rute schrieb:

What is the input to these kernels? Lean code (pre-compiled)? oleans? Exported proofs? I ask, because we know some input forms are more susceptible to hacks.

Exported proofs, in the new JSON based format that safely encodes strings.

For now the arena will focus on checkers. A nice safe walled garden where all you have to worry about whether a certain text file with an exported is proof is good or bad. It's only one puzzle piece in the overall story, but I think it help to keep separate concerns separate.

I think it is very reasonable to start with exported proofs and external checkers. It seems like it would be very hard to piece apart into a similar benchmark the trust apportioned to oleans or proof export that is assumed for all but the most adversarial of input.
Incidentally, why is Nanoda almost twice as fast as the Lean kernel at checking Mathlib?

James E Hanson said:

Incidentally, why is Nanoda almost twice as fast as the Lean kernel at checking Mathlib?

It only has to do this one thing, so it's able to get away with more spartan data structures and memory management strategies. I think using deBruijn levels instead of unique identifiers for free variables also helps with caching in some spots but that's more speculative.
Or maybe Chris is just a great programmer :-)

Kernel Arena Update

Allow me to share some updates on the kernel arena at https://arena.lean-lang.org/

The Arena now sports 5 separate checkers:

  • The official kernel (in various versions)
  • @Mario Carneiro’s lean4lean
  • @Chris Bailey’s nanoda
  • A naive kernel implementation in Lean by me, the mini-kernel
  • A WIP kernel in Python by @Julian Berman called rpylean

The first three are serious, complete kernel implementations that correctly pass all the tests on the arena (not all at the same time, though, see below).

The kernel arena also comes with a the Kernel Tutorial Tests, a sequence of small test inputs (both good and bad) that exercise some aspects of a checker. The idea is that if you want to write a checker and don’t know where to start, just follow these tests in sequence and expand/fix your implementation to get the next one green. I have created a Verso-based rendering of these tests for easy inspection (@Julian Berman may currently be most interested in this).

Writing these checks has already helped to uncover and fix issues in the two external checkers.

The mini kernel does not support all of lean, but for the fragment it supports it should be sound. It probably isn’t, so if you enjoy breaking things, please do find the holes in this, as every hole here is a missing test case in the tutorial. If you find one, I’ll owe you a drink at the next lean event! (I know that I am not checking for duplicate declarations yet, as that is a bit tricky with the way the test files are generated. Besides that I made some implementation choices there that are “risky”, and just because I can’t exploit it yet doesn’t mean you cannot; see the README)

Currently the arena runs all checkers on all tests in one go to update the page. Takes 6h (on a rather weak virtual machine). I manually run that when something interesting has changed, not on every commit, though.

Two issues so far:

  • At some point I had everything on versions that lean4lean liked, but when I bumped some tests to get fixes in a proof that makes nanoda accept it, lean4lean started to stumble again (hence the “declined” tests), presumably until that Lean version gets released and lean4lean adjusted.

    I expect things to start to settle, though. I hope that once we have a stable release that works with all checkers, we can update at a more sensible pace (e.g. to the next stable release as soon as all checkers had time to adjust, if needed).

  • The specification for external checkers is not clear. Is it simply the official kernel, including all possible incompletenesses or other strange corner case behavior? How should we treat tests where a different result is also reasonable, in some way? For example @Arthur Adjedj has proposed some clean-ups to the kernel, and it would be nice to test that on the arena. One option is to somehow add a label to the test that this is testing an “alternative world”, and tally/present such tests differently.

The export JSON format is not very human-readable. Every syntactic node in every expression has its own entry and entries refer to each other by number rather than by name.

For example, the exported version of Nat.add_succ is 572 lines long and I believe this essentially just contains the same information as the theorem declaration

@[defeq] theorem Nat.add_succ : ∀ (n m : ℕ), n + m.succ = (n + m).succ :=
fun n m => rfl

and the reduced proof term

fun n m => Eq.refl ((Nat.rec ⟨fun x => x, PUnit.unit⟩ (fun n n_ih => ⟨fun x => (n_ih.1 x).succ, n_ih⟩) m).1 n).succ
And all declarations that are used in the transitive closure of constants
Right, but there aren't that many for Nat.add_succ, right?
The only user-level things I'm seeing are constants related to Nat, Eq, HAdd, Add, PUnit, and PProd.

Jason Rute said:

Is there a clear sense of what the slowest parts of the existing kernels are (for say practical purposes like checking mathlib)?

There's a lot of time spent just doing substitution and otherwise traversing terms, which I don't think you can really optimize around. The main alternative is using something closure-based, but because lean's reduction is typed, I don't think there's a good way to implement something like Rocq's vm_compute (or really any good closure based solution whether eager or lazy) for Lean. I wrote a version that uses a krivine machine out of curiosity (and because I was not aware of the problems arising out of typed reduction), but you need to readback/quote the terms too often to get any kind of advantage. It feels like there should be some kind of parallel solution to readback, but I assume this is not possible as no one's done it yet.

The high performing strategies on benchmarks like smalltt seem to all have issues that make them unsuitable for use with Lean's type theory, at least not without some new discoveries.

Do you mean Rocq' cbv or Lean's new cbv? The latter could be described like a more predictable simp, and produces proofs using rewriting.

The high performing strategies on benchmarks like smalltt seem to all have issues that make them unsuitable for use with Lean's type theory, at least not without some new discoveries.

https://github.com/intgrah/sokonanoda/tree/master
I have implemented a type checker using NbE, and it seems to be pretty successful. It is 35% faster than still-nanoda (58% faster, if you ignore parsing). I actually skip the quote/readback step, as in Coquand's original algorithm, and this preserves the "glued" values to assist with value-domain comparison. Quoting is only used for pretty printing. I use typed neutrals as in Abel-Coquand-Dybjer, which smalltt seems to not do, and it pretty much just works for Lean's type theory.
I haven't yet experimented with different speculation strategies for conversion, nor has NbE fully replaced the old algorithm in places other than conversion checking. There's also likely some room for improvement regarding hashing, caching, and (de)allocation.

Amazing!

How does NbE interact with lazy unfolding (i.e. checking a =?= b when facing f a =? f b)? Does it do that? Can it follow the same heuristics that the Lean kernel uses, or does it proceed differently but still handles practical proofs out there just fine?

Yes, f a =? f b is handled lazily, roughly following the same heuristics as the Lean kernel; congruence followed by height-ordered reducibility hinted unfolding. Just in the value domain, so heads + spines

This might be a stupid question, but I've noticed that you can disable the kernel with set_option debug.skipKernelTC true and Lean seems to mostly work fine and it still gives you type errors where expected. So the elaborator has its own typechecker that it runs before feeding your code to the actual kernel typechecker. (Not sure if this typechecking only happens during the Syntax -> Expr translation of it can be made to work on already elaborated expressions.) Does this mean that the elaborator is a sort of "untrusted second kernel", and if so, would it be possible to add it to the arena? It wouldn't need to reject all bad inputs, but knowing where it disagrees with the actual kernel could be useful.

Niels Voss said:

This might be a stupid question, but I've noticed that you can disable the kernel with set_option debug.skipKernelTC true and Lean seems to mostly work fine and it still gives you type errors where expected. So the elaborator has its own typechecker that it runs before feeding your code to the actual kernel typechecker. (Not sure if this typechecking only happens during the Syntax -> Expr translation of it can be made to work on already elaborated expressions.) Does this mean that the elaborator is a sort of "untrusted second kernel", and if so, would it be possible to add it to the arena? It wouldn't need to reject all bad inputs, but knowing where it disagrees with the actual kernel could be useful.

I don't see why not. I think the elaborator is designed to be more permissive than the kernel, so it would be good to quantify the amount of unsoundness, if any, permitted by it. Some things which are kernel-only, like inductive soundness and recursor generation, will still have to call the actual kernel, but those are only minor.

Joachim Breitner said:

I may have to rethink the ordering.

I think "rejections don't matter if you parse mathlib" would be a reasonable change: just do percentage-accept and percentage-reject as the primary sort, and :prohibited: is only accounted for as a tiebreaker if you don't handle mathlib at all. All four top kernels get it right when they don't decline, and they don't decline mathlib, so they're equivalent on the exit code where it matters.

Niels Voss said:

(Not sure if this typechecking only happens during the Syntax -> Expr translation of it can be made to work on already elaborated expressions.) Does this mean that the elaborator is a sort of "untrusted second kernel", and if so, would it be possible to add it to the arena?

Elaboration pretty definitionally acts on syntax, not elaborated expressions, so what I think you'd have to do is use Lean's delaborator to turn Exprs back into text, and then feed those back in through the parsing and evaluation pipeline. My hunch is that would amount to a pretty significant test of Lean's delaborator and probably a pretty simple test of Lean's elaborator. In other words, if I was betting I'd bet you'd be likely to find a lot of corner cases in the delaborator that aren't going to be worth the effort to fix, and unlikely to find bugs in the elaborator, which is only being asked to re-parse things that the delaborator understood.

Perhaps someone else has a different design in mind!

Rob Simmons said:

Elaboration pretty definitionally acts on syntax, not elaborated expressions, so what I think you'd have to do is use Lean's delaborator to turn Exprs back into text, and then feed those back in through the parsing and evaluation pipeline. My hunch is that would amount to a pretty significant test of Lean's delaborator and probably a pretty simple test of Lean's elaborator.

The elaborator starts from Syntax, but its type checking is on Expr. So I'd have thought you wouldn't need the delaborator at all.
Hmm, good point.

Yes, you could use docs#Lean.Meta.check. But it might be a lot less efficient (since it's not specifically optimized to be a kernel and has to account for metavariables and everything). More importantly though, the elaborator doesn't cover everything, for example I don't think we have an algorithm for producing the recursor of inductives.

I think Rob is right that the elaborator checking is a Syntax → Expr operation. Meta.check is just another tool that is available to the elaborator. What would be possible is to delaborate the expression with set_option pp.all true and then to elaborate the result, which avoids delaboration edge cases. But Meta.check will be a lot more efficient than that.

Ok so bumping cedar completely exploded my kernel (sokonanoda) because of memory usage, going up to about 14GB. I think I've found out why but there were so many red herrings along the way.

The culprit declaration is TermPrimType.lt_trans in https://github.com/cedar-policy/cedar-spec/blob/2d7da594c2163ece2cdc7f4f51bf281684f442da/cedar-lean/Cedar/Thm/SymCC/Data/LT.lean#L123. This declaration is mostly innocent, but the size issue comes from the use of cases a <;> cases b <;> cases c, resulting in 125 cases, 64 of which are relevant to the slowdown.
The elaborated output of this proof uses docs#ByteArray.utf8Decode?. In lean4#11416, 4.27.0, this definition went from using fuel, to using well founded recursion. Well founded recursion is known to be slow in the kernel, but it is especially slow for my checker, because interning isn't possible here for the following reason.

In Lean, well founded recursion is defined using accessibility (docs#Acc). However the computation ("iota") rule is

example
    {α : Sort v} {r : α → α → Prop}
    {motive : (a : α) → Acc r a → Sort u}
    (intro :
        (x : α) →
        (h : (y : α) → r y x → Acc r y) →
        ((y : α) → (a : r y x) → motive y (h y a)) →
        motive x (Acc.intro x h))
    (x : α)
    (h : (y : α) → r y x → Acc r y) :
    Acc.rec intro (Acc.intro x h) =
    intro x h (fun y a => Acc.rec intro (h y a)) :=
  rfl

And note that fun y a => ... is a lambda. In NbE, evaluating a lambda produces a closure, so y and a get captured in the environment. This unfortunately means that every step of the recursion produces lambda terms paired with distinct environments, thus they are non-identical closures and cannot be interned.
This, combined with the 64x multiplier in the proof, and the fact that my typechecker (and nanoda and others) do not free memory in the middle of checking a declaration, means that my checker explodes here.

One of the big red herrings was the import all statement, added when cedar adopted the module system. I had thought that this changed some reducibility depth hints, leading my checker to take an incorrect reduction path many times over.

Interesting insight! But I’m surprised it’s using Acc; if the measure is Nat, since https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/commit/f9dc77673b5b4746b825d1d07f4d1fb200b8f5ec (PR #7965) it should be using WellFounded.Nat.fix, which should be nicer?
You're right, it is using WellFounded.Nat.fix actually, but I think the same thing about lambda capturing applies.

Ok yes, the computation rule is still 

go (Nat.succ fuel) x hfuel
    = s fuel (go fuel) x hfuel
    = F x (fun y hy => go fuel y (Nat.lt_of_lt_of_le hy (Nat.le_of_lt_add_one hfuel)))

where the build time is spent

No timeouts were hit anywhere in this run — the 9-hour wall clock is genuinely spent by slow-but-succeeding checkers, running strictly sequentially. Here's the breakdown.

Where the time goes

Of the 9 h 2 m job, the steps split as: Build checkers 16 min, Generate tests 22 min, Run checkers on tests 8 h 20 min, everything else a few minutes. Within the run step, the sum of the per-run reported times is 8.27 h — i.e. the runs execute one at a time with essentially no overhead and no parallelism (consistent with the recent revert: parallel-run (#84) commit).

By test, the big-export tests dominate: mathlib 351 min, cslib 68 min, std 41 min, cedar 20 min — together 480 of ~496 minutes. By checker:

Checker Total Biggest single run
lean4lean 164 min mathlib: 2.3 h (accepted, correct)
rpylean 123 min mathlib: 54 min — rejected, wrong result
official-v4.28.0 59 min mathlib: 48 min
official 48 min mathlib: 38 min
official-nightly 48 min mathlib: 38 min
all others combined ~55 min nanobruijn mathlib 10 min, nanoda 9 min, …

Answer to your question: no bad-timeout offenders

The checkers that can't handle mathlib all exit fast, so timeouts aren't the problem:

  • mini and evmlean decline mathlib instantly (⊘, <1 s).
  • nyaya errors out after 14 s, vow-lean-kernel after 30 s (it has its own 30 s timeout wrapper, working as intended).
  • nanobruijn's 3600 s timeout exists but it finishes mathlib in 10 min, so it's never hit.
  • No ⏱/timed-out result appears anywhere in the log.

The one arguably wasted chunk is rpylean on mathlib: 54 minutes to produce an incorrect rejection (:-1: :cross_mark:). That's not a timeout — it runs to completion and gives the wrong answer — but if it deterministically fails on mathlib, those 54 min buy nothing and could be skipped or capped in checkers/rpylean.yaml.

The two real levers for the wall clock are structural, not timeout-related: lean4lean alone spends 2.3 h on mathlib (28% of the run step, a legitimate success — it's just slow), and the sequential execution means every checker's mathlib run adds up linearly. Re-enabling some form of parallelism (perhaps only for non-perf/ tests, if the revert was about timing fidelity) would help far more than tightening any timeout.

From one of the examples in @Mario Carneiro's thesis:

variable {P : Prop} {r : P → P → Prop}
  {α : Sort 1} (f : P → α) (h : ∀ x y, r x y → f x = f y)
  (q : Quot r) (z : P)

theorem left : Quot.lift f h q = Quot.lift f h (Quot.mk r z) :=
  rfl

theorem right : Quot.lift f h (Quot.mk r z) = f z :=
  rfl

theorem trans : Quot.lift f h q = f z :=
  rfl

His thesis says that algorithmic equality validates left and right but not trans. However the kernel right now actually rejects left. I can believe that at some point, the kernel did accept left. This also isn't one of those cases where we have a clearly marked algorithmic equality that's precisely specified as a decidable subset of declarative equality, because left ought to be algorithmically decidable using the usual rules:

congr_app (refl : Quot.lift f h ≡ Quot.lift f h) (proof_irrel : q ≡ Quot.mk r z)

The official kernel here does WHNF reducing the RHS to f z, before congr_app.
Of course, Lean's type theory is unspecified, so one could argue this is not an incompleteness bug, but an incompleteness feature like the rest, but I think the premise (specifying the type theory) needs to be fixed :)
Yup - and until that's fixed we'll just live with that completeness is somewhat vagu and pragmatic on the arena. Tests that don't prescribe a particular outcome serve that purpose.

I've also thought a bit about how the recursor information can actually be very useful. While it's pretty clear how to derive the recursor from a mutual inductive declaration, deriving the recursor for a nested inductive exposes a lot of implementation details: How are the motives ordered? How are the special nested recursors named? Which nested parts are considered equal? (see also lean4#9029) So if you want to be compatible with the official kernel and are just given the constructor types and the inductive type type, you essentially have to copy what it's doing, i.e. how it's traversing the constructors etc.

But instead, you might as well look at the recursors, right? In there you can directly read off how the motives are ordered and you can infer the names by looking at how the recursors correspond to motives in their return value. You can even infer all the inductive type types and constructor types from just a single recursor! So you could almost argue that the constructor and inductive type types and names should be a "comment" and the real information would be the first recursor. And you could also implement your checker to generate the induction type based on just that first recursor and validate the "redundant" information that is the constructors, the inductive type itself and every but one recursor.

So, I think the recursor information is indeed very useful and it opens up paths for checkers to be more reliable when faced with nested inductives. In fact, I think that's what I would use for inductives in the kernel (if I ever got to writing a kernel lol). Of course, that also means you gotta be a bit more careful since the information you're given is more complex.

indeed, I've been thinking of doing something like this for the specification as well: you provide a coverage of all the nested types and the kernel checks your list is complete and gives you motives in the order you specify

Okay, here are the three issues I identified! Each has the source (the .ndjson or .lean), and some explanation.

One of them 01 causes a panic when Eq is declared with a _different constructor name_ than usual, like Eq.mk instead of Eq.refl. This is apparently "allowed" (in some sense), but then causes an assertion failure when the quot module is loaded. This one can be done with plain .lean, but it requires skipping prelude. It causes nanoda to panic with an assert, which is not super graceful. Not a big deal, but it's something nanoda does differently than the official kernel or lean4lean.

The second, 02, happens when an axiom has an unused universe parameter. This is explicitly _not_ permitted by the Lean elaborator, so can't come about from plain Lean source, but should(?) be a valid ndjson file. It causes nanoda to Option::unwrap() on a None value and panic.

The third, 03, genuinely gets nanoda to accept a theorem boom : False and report no axioms used. It can't be prepared from a .lean file, though, the lean4export'er can't produce this it seems. It's also not accepted by lean4lean or the official kernel.

I think it's worth noting: none of these were found in the process of bug-hunting. I just set up an agent to moderately-adversarially devise tricky test cases to compare my in-development kernel against the three existing ones, and in the process it happened across these three places they diverge anyway.
